Lecture 1 · The qubit §1.2 States are rays

1 Do 12(∣0⟩+i∣1⟩)\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ii\ket1)2​1​(∣0⟩+i∣1⟩) and 12(i∣0⟩−∣1⟩)\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ii\ket0-\ket1)2​1​(i∣0⟩−∣1⟩) describe the same state?

Here is the hint — try once more. Postulate 1.1: two unit vectors describe the same state exactly when ψ′=eiηψ\psi'=e^{\ii\eta}\psiψ′=eiηψ with η\etaη real. Try eiη=ie^{\ii\eta}=\iieiη=i. i⋅12(∣0⟩+i∣1⟩)=12(i∣0⟩−∣1⟩)\ii\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ii\ket1)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ii\ket0-\ket1)i⋅2​1​(∣0⟩+i∣1⟩)=2​1​(i∣0⟩−∣1⟩), so the two vectors differ by the phase i=eiπ/2\ii=e^{\ii\pi/2}i=eiπ/2 and describe one state, for every measurement (Postulate 1.1). Lecture 1 · The qubit §1.7 A state holds probabilities, not values

6 For H=c11+ℏν2σzH=c\Id+\tfrac{\hbar\freq}2\sigma_zH=c11+2ℏν​σz​ with ν>0\freq>0ν>0, and a state away from the poles, the point r\blochvr turns about ez\mathbf e_zez​. What does this say about the energy readings?

Here is the hint — try once more. The energy readings are c±ℏν2c\pm\tfrac{\hbar\freq}2c±2ℏν​, and their probabilities depend only on rzr_zrz​ (Corollary 1.8). Does the turning change rzr_zrz​? The readings c±ℏν2c\pm\tfrac{\hbar\freq}2c±2ℏν​ have probabilities 12(1±rz)\tfrac12(1\pm r_z)21​(1±rz​) (Corollary 1.8), and the turn about ez\mathbf e_zez​ keeps rzr_zrz​ (Theorem 1.12). Lecture 1 · The qubit §1.4 Observables and measurement

7 Two states have Bloch vectors (0.6,0,0.8)(0.6,0,0.8)(0.6,0,0.8) and (0,0.6,0.8)(0,0.6,0.8)(0,0.6,0.8). Which measurement cannot tell them apart, however many copies you measure?

Here is the hint — try once more. By Born's rule on the sphere, a measurement along m\mvecm sees only m⋅r\mvec\cdot\blochvm⋅r. Compute it for each axis. Along zzz both have m⋅r=0.8\mvec\cdot\blochv=0.8m⋅r=0.8, so both read +1+1+1 with probability 0.90.90.9: they lie on one circle of latitude about zzz (Remark 1.9). Along xxx the components are 0.60.60.6 and 000 (probabilities 0.80.80.8 and 0.50.50.5), and along yyy they are 000 and 0.60.60.6.

Lecture 1 · The qubit §1.4 Observables and measurement

8 A qubit in ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ is measured along xxx, and the reading is +1+1+1. At once, with no time to evolve, it is measured along zzz. With what probability does this second reading give +1+1+1?

Lüders' rule: after the reading +1+1+1 along xxx, where is the Bloch vector? Then apply Born's rule along zzz.

Here is the hint — try once more. After the reading +1+1+1 along xxx the state is ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩, at ex\mathbf e_xex​ (Corollary 1.8), whose component along zzz is 000; so Prob⁡(+1)=12(1+0)=0.5\Prob(+1)=\tfrac12(1+0)=0.5Prob(+1)=21​(1+0)=0.5. The first reading replaced the state ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩, for which a zzz reading would have given +1+1+1 with certainty.

The Bloch vector precesses about the unit vector n\nvecn along (Ω,0,ν0)(\Omega,0,\freq_0)(Ω,0,ν0​) and keeps n⋅r\nvec\cdot\blochvn⋅r (§2.1). How low can it get?

The circle about n\nvecn through ez\mathbf e_zez​ reaches down to rz=cos⁡2αr_z=\cos2\alpharz​=cos2α, so the probability of ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ is at most sin⁡2α=Ω2/(Ω2+ν02)=110\sin^2\alpha=\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\freq_0^2)=\tfrac1{10}sin2α=Ω2/(Ω2+ν02​)=101​ (§2.1). The square of the ratio alone is 19≈0.111\tfrac19\approx0.11191​≈0.111, and sin⁡α≈0.316\sin\alpha\approx0.316sinα≈0.316 is not squared.

Lecture 2 · A driven qubit: magnetic resonance §2.2 A Hamiltonian that changes in time

Here is the hint — try once more. At t=π/(2ν)t=\pi/(2\freq)t=π/(2ν) the transverse field has turned through the angle νt=π/2\freq t=\pi/2νt=π/2. What are its cosine and sine? At νt=π/2\freq t=\pi/2νt=π/2, cos⁡(νt)=0\cos(\freq t)=0cos(νt)=0 and sin⁡(νt)=1\sin(\freq t)=1sin(νt)=1, so (2.1) gives H=ℏ2(ν0σz+Ωσy)H=\tfrac\hbar2(\freq_0\sigma_z+\Omega\sigma_y)H=2ℏ​(ν0​σz​+Ωσy​): the transverse field has turned from xxx to yyy. Lecture 2 · A driven qubit: magnetic resonance §2.7 Circular and linear drives

7 A linear drive is the sum of two circular parts that turn in opposite senses. In the rotating frame of the first part, how does the second part move?

Here is the hint — try once more. In the laboratory the second part turns at the rate ν\freqν clockwise, and the frame turns at the rate ν\freqν anticlockwise (Remark 2.5). In the frame the second part is ℏΩ2(cos⁡(2νt) σx−sin⁡(2νt) σy)\tfrac{\hbar\Omega}2\bigl(\cos(2\freq t)\,\sigma_x-\sin(2\freq t)\,\sigma_y\bigr)2ℏΩ​(cos(2νt)σx​−sin(2νt)σy​) (Remark 2.5). Its angle is −2νt-2\freq t−2νt, so it turns at the rate 2ν2\freq2ν, clockwise seen from the tip of ez\mathbf e_zez​. In the laboratory it turns at the rate ν\freqν clockwise, and the frame adds its own rate ν\freqν. Dropping this part is the rotating-wave approximation.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.1 An unpolarised beam

1 A beam reads +1+1+1 along zzz with probability 12\tfrac1221​, and along xxx with probability 111. Can it be the beam from the oven?

Here is the hint — try once more. The beam from the oven reads +1+1+1 with probability 12\tfrac1221​ along every axis (§3.1). The beam from the oven gives 12\tfrac1221​ along every axis, and this beam gives 111 along xxx, so it is not that beam (§3.1). The equal mixture of ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ and ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ gives 12\tfrac1221​ along xxx.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.2 Random preparations

2 An ensemble has ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ with probability 14\tfrac1441​ and ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ with probability 34\tfrac3443​. An atom from it reads +1+1+1 along xxx. With what probability was it prepared ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩? (Give a decimal.)

First the law of total probability (3.1) for the reading, then Bayes' rule (3.2).

Here is the hint — try once more. Each member reads +1+1+1 along xxx with probability 12\tfrac1221​, so by (3.1) Prob⁡(+1)=14⋅12+34⋅12=12\Prob(+1)=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12Prob(+1)=41​⋅21​+43​⋅21​=21​, and by Bayes' rule (3.2) Prob⁡(↑∣+1)=14⋅12/12=14\Prob(\uparrow\mid+1)=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12/\tfrac12=\tfrac14Prob(↑∣+1)=41​⋅21​/21​=41​. Both members give this reading equally often, so it does not change the weights. The probability of "prepared ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ and read +1+1+1" is 18\tfrac1881​.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.3 The density matrix

3 An ensemble is {(12,∣↑⟩),(12,∣+x⟩)}\{(\tfrac12,\ket\uparrow),(\tfrac12,\ket{+x})\}{(21​,∣↑⟩),(21​,∣+x⟩)}. Find its density matrix, and use it to find the probability of +1+1+1 along zzz. (Give a decimal.)

ρ=12∣↑⟩ ⁣⟨↑∣+12∣+x⟩ ⁣⟨+x∣\rho=\tfrac12\proj\uparrow+\tfrac12\proj{+x}ρ=21​∣↑⟩⟨↑∣+21​∣+x⟩⟨+x∣ (Definition 3.3), and one reading with projection EEE has probability Tr⁡(ρE)\Tr(\rho E)Tr(ρE) (Theorem 3.4). Here E=∣↑⟩ ⁣⟨↑∣E=\proj\uparrowE=∣↑⟩⟨↑∣.

Here is the hint — try once more. Every entry of ∣+x⟩ ⁣⟨+x∣\proj{+x}∣+x⟩⟨+x∣ is 12\tfrac1221​, so ρ\rhoρ has the rows (34,14)(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)(43​,41​) and (14,14)(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)(41​,41​), and Tr⁡(ρ∣↑⟩ ⁣⟨↑∣)=34\Tr(\rho\proj\uparrow)=\tfrac34Tr(ρ∣↑⟩⟨↑∣)=43​ (Theorem 3.4). Member by member, 12⋅1+12⋅12=34\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac3421​⋅1+21​⋅21​=43​. The pure state halfway between, at (ex+ez)/2(\mathbf e_x+\mathbf e_z)/\sqrt2(ex​+ez​)/2​, would give 12(1+12)≈0.854\tfrac12\bigl(1+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)\approx0.85421​(1+2​1​)≈0.854.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.4 The Bloch ball

4 A density matrix ρ\rhoρ has the rows (34,14)(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)(43​,41​) and (14,14)(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)(41​,41​). What is its larger eigenvalue? (Give a decimal.)

Find its Bloch vector ra=Tr⁡ρσar_a=\Tr\rho\sigma_ara​=Trρσa​, and use Theorem 3.6: the eigenvalues are 12(1±∣r∣)\tfrac12(1\pm\abs{\blochv})21​(1±∣r∣).

Here is the hint — try once more. Here rx=2⋅14=12r_x=2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12rx​=2⋅41​=21​, ry=0r_y=0ry​=0 and rz=34−14=12r_z=\tfrac34-\tfrac14=\tfrac12rz​=43​−41​=21​, so ∣r∣=1/2\abs{\blochv}=1/\sqrt2∣r∣=1/2​, and the eigenvalues are 12(1±12)\tfrac12\bigl(1\pm\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)21​(1±2​1​), the larger ≈0.854\approx0.854≈0.854 (Theorem 3.6). The diagonal entry 34\tfrac3443​ is not an eigenvalue, since ρ\rhoρ is not diagonal. Also Tr⁡ρ2=12(1+12)=34\Tr\rho^2=\tfrac12\bigl(1+\tfrac12\bigr)=\tfrac34Trρ2=21​(1+21​)=43​.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.5 A worked example

5 In Example 3.8, after the quarter turn, the reading along xxx is −1-1−1. What is the state afterwards, and how was the atom prepared, in the first ensemble (∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ with probability 0.80.80.8, ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ with probability 0.20.20.2)?

Here is the hint — try once more. The quarter turn takes ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ to ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩ and ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ to ∣−x⟩\ket{-x}∣−x⟩. Which member can read −1-1−1? Then use Bayes' rule. The reading −1-1−1 along xxx leaves the pure state ∣−x⟩\ket{-x}∣−x⟩, whatever the density matrix was (§3.4). Only the member turned to ∣−x⟩\ket{-x}∣−x⟩, the one prepared ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩, can give it, so by Bayes' rule the atom was prepared ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ with probability 0.2⋅1/0.2=10.2\cdot1/0.2=10.2⋅1/0.2=1. Conditioning changes the weights (Remark 3.5). The reading itself has probability 12(1−0.6)=0.2\tfrac12(1-0.6)=0.221​(1−0.6)=0.2.

Lecture 3 · Mixtures and the Bloch ball §3.3 The density matrix

6 Can any experiment distinguish the equal mixture of ∣+y⟩\ket{+y}∣+y⟩ and ∣−y⟩\ket{-y}∣−y⟩ from the beam from the oven?

Here is the hint — try once more. Compute the density matrix of the mixture, and use Theorem 3.4. 12∣+y⟩ ⁣⟨+y∣+12∣−y⟩ ⁣⟨−y∣=1211\tfrac12\proj{+y}+\tfrac12\proj{-y}=\tfrac12\Id21​∣+y⟩⟨+y∣+21​∣−y⟩⟨−y∣=21​11, the density matrix of the beam from the oven, so by Theorem 3.4 every experiment gives both the same probabilities. Along yyy both read +1+1+1 with probability 12\tfrac1221​, and in both a repeated reading repeats. A density matrix does not record which states were mixed (§3.6).

7 The state ∣+x⟩=12(∣↑⟩+∣↓⟩)\ket{+x}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket\uparrow+\ket\downarrow)∣+x⟩=2​1​(∣↑⟩+∣↓⟩) and the equal mixture of ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ and ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ are measured along one axis. Which axis tells them apart?

Here is the hint — try once more. The mixture has r=0\blochv=0r=0, and ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩ has r=ex\blochv=\mathbf e_xr=ex​. The state ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩ has r=ex\blochv=\mathbf e_xr=ex​: along xxx it reads +1+1+1 with certainty, and along zzz and yyy with probability 12\tfrac1221​, like the mixture.
